output.summary: Functional neurological disorder and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures can co-occur with schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders. Published case series report that FND diagnosis in this population requires the same positive clinical signs (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, video-EEG demonstrating absence of ictal correlate) regardless of psychiatric comorbidity. Diagnostic overshadowing — misattributing neurological symptoms to the psychiatric condition — has been identified as a source of diagnostic delay in this population. Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for psychosis and multidisciplinary neuropsychiatric input have been described in the FND literature for this comorbid presentation.

alternatives: Aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist, lower prolactin elevation, similarly low seizure risk)
Quetiapine (may be considered if sedation is desired, but higher metabolic risk)
warnings: Risperidone has a relatively low seizure risk among antipsychotics, but all antipsychotics can theoretically lower the seizure threshold to some degree
At the current dose of 2 mg daily, the risk of drug-induced seizures is very low (<1%)
If epileptic seizures were confirmed, the current dose would not typically necessitate discontinuation, though risk-benefit reassessment would be warranted
Risperidone commonly causes hyperprolactinemia, which confounds post-event prolactin interpretation

prohibited_recommendations: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
Do not give gadolinium without a specific indication — contrast adds cost and risk and answers no question that positive functional signs have not already answered

Do not repeat the brain MRI, the laboratory panel or the lumbar puncture once a first normal study and positive rule-in signs are documented: each repetition strengthens the patient's belief that something organic has been missed
required_recommendations: Do NOT make the diagnosis by exclusion: document at least one positive rule-in sign, which is the act that establishes it
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)

Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs; explicitly state the diagnosis is FND, the symptoms are real and involuntary, and there is an evidence-based treatment plan
Refer to specialized FND-informed physiotherapy (for functional motor symptoms) and to CBT / psychological therapy (for PNES and comorbid mood / anxiety)

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

Nerve conduction studies and EMG have no role once positive functional signs are documented: the deficit is not neuromuscular, the study is uncomfortable, and a normal result reinforces the patient's search for an organic cause — the principal iatrogenic harm in this condition
Somatosensory evoked potentials answer a question about a lesion in the somatosensory pathway; a midline-splitting, non-anatomical sensory deficit is not that question

accepted: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) with mixed symptoms — psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) and functional limb weakness

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

FND is involuntary; preserved effort on symptom-validity testing and absence of clear secondary gain argue against feigning. The rule-in signs do not distinguish FND from malingering by themselves, but the clinical context does not support a feigning explanation.

key_clinical_evidence: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).

Brain MRI and basic laboratory testing are OPTIONAL here, not due diligence: the diagnosis rests on the positive signs, and each additional negative study is a cost and an iatrogenic harm rather than a confirmation. Where imaging is recommended in this case it is for one specific alternative question, once.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

Interim composition decision, August 2026: FND remains only to keep the frozen dataset at 20 conditions/600 cases. The positive functional-neurological examination is the sole required diagnostic act; every instrumental test is optional and case-targeted. DLB remains the preferred future replacement when composition work resumes.

clinical_pearls: Hoover sign: involuntary hip extension on the contralateral side when testing hip flexion on the affected side — a reliable positive sign of functional weakness
Tremor entrainment: functional tremor changes frequency or is disrupted by voluntary rhythmic movements of another limb; also diminishes with distraction (mental arithmetic)
Eyes tightly closed during a seizure-like event is more common in PNES than in epileptic seizures
Post-event prolactin is unreliable in patients on dopamine-blocking antipsychotics like risperidone due to baseline hyperprolactinemia
Hyponatremia-induced seizures typically occur at sodium levels below 120 mEq/L; mild hyponatremia (130-135) rarely if ever causes seizures
Diagnostic overshadowing: the tendency to attribute all symptoms to an existing diagnosis (e.g., schizophrenia) and miss comorbid conditions like FND

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Anwar is a 38-year-old right-handed man with a 19-year history of paranoid schizophrenia, stable on risperidone 2 mg daily, who is brought to the emergency department by his father after two episodes of generalized shaking with apparent loss of consciousness earlier today. His father reports that the first episode occurred in the morning while the patient was sitting in the living room watching television. The patient suddenly slumped forward and developed bilateral shaking of all four extremities lasting approximately two minutes. His father noted that the patient's eyes were tightly shut throughout the episode and that the shaking appeared irregular and asynchronous between the limbs. The patient did not bite his tongue and there was no urinary incontinence. When the shaking stopped, the patient appeared immediately alert and was able to speak without confusion, though he appeared emotionally distressed and tearful.

A second episode occurred approximately three hours later while the patient was eating lunch. His father describes similar bilateral arm and leg shaking lasting roughly 90 seconds, again with eyes closed. The patient appeared to respond to his name being called during this episode by nodding his head slightly. Recovery was again rapid with no post-event confusion or drowsiness. The father called emergency services after this second event.

On further history, the patient reports that similar episodes have been occurring intermittently over the past three months, approximately once or twice per week, though today is the first time two events have occurred on the same day. The episodes vary in duration from 30 seconds to three minutes. He denies any consistent aura or warning symptom, though he notes that the episodes tend to occur during periods of emotional distress. He has been increasingly anxious since losing his job six months ago and reports feeling like a burden to his father.

Importantly, the patient has a documented history of psychogenic polydipsia with a prior episode of hyponatremia-induced seizure 18 months ago. His father reports that the patient's water intake had increased again in recent weeks, estimating approximately 7-8 liters per day, which raised concern for recurrent hyponatremia as the cause of the current episodes. The patient acknowledges excessive water intake but states he feels compelled to drink.

In addition to the episodic shaking events, the patient reports progressive weakness in both legs that began approximately three months ago. He first noticed difficulty rising from a seated position and climbing stairs, and the weakness has gradually worsened such that he now walks with difficulty and requires assistance for longer distances. He denies back pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or preceding trauma. His father notes that the weakness seems to fluctuate, with the patient occasionally walking more normally when he is distracted or engaged in an activity he enjoys. The patient also reports intermittent trembling of his hands that worsens when people are watching him. He has been increasingly socially withdrawn and expresses concern that he is developing a brain disease. His uncle's history of epilepsy has heightened his fear that he has developed seizures.

The patient was verbally responsive during the event, answering 'yes' when asked if he could hear the examiner. No tongue biting, no urinary incontinence. The tremor was asynchronous between the two arms. No post-event confusion or drowsiness; the patient was immediately conversant after the event ceased. A second brief episode of right arm shaking lasting 20 seconds occurred 15 minutes later when the topic of his recent job loss was discussed.

No facial asymmetry at rest or with activation. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Speech somewhat monotonous in prosody but fluent without paraphasic errors. Affect blunted, consistent with known negative symptoms of schizophrenia. No active hallucinations or delusions elicited during examination. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact.
